confidence_note: The book's framework recalled and cross-checked with general coverage, not page-checked: the Great Rewiring around 2010 to 2015, the four norms, the collective action argument. Omitted as unverified: precise statistics, the iPhone 4 front-camera detail, names of cited studies. Haidt's causal claim is disputed by some researchers; the story says so. No single anecdote; the book's example is the shift in childhood itself.
facts: Haidt describes a Great Rewiring of childhood between about 2010 and 2015: from a play-based childhood to a phone-based one.
He reports that teen anxiety, depression and self-harm rose sharply in the early 2010s, especially among girls.
He names two changes: children lost unsupervised play in the real world, and smartphones and social media took over their time.
Haidt argues a family cannot solve this alone: a child without a phone is left out when everyone else is on one, a collective action problem.
His proposed norms: no smartphone before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools, and far more unsupervised play and independence.
Some researchers dispute that phones are the cause; the evidence is mostly correlational.
Haidt says children became overprotected in the real world and underprotected online.
He names four harms of the phone-based childhood: social deprivation, sleep deprivation, attention fragmentation and addiction.
scene_details: a child left out because every classmate is in a group chat
a school where phones are locked away during the day
tension: One family can say no, but its child pays for it alone.
opening_idea: Open on the child whose parents say no to a phone while the whole class is already in the group chat.

lessons.idea: A rule that is hard to keep alone becomes easy when a whole group agrees on it together.
lessons.anchor: the child left out when only one family holds the line; phone-free schools as shared rule

reflect_final: Which habit is hard for you to change alone, and who around you could agree on one shared rule for it with you this month?

use_cases.situation: Parents at a school group are unsure about phones.
use_cases.move: Propose one shared rule for the class, such as no phones before a certain age.

use_cases.situation: A team inbox drains everybody after hours.
use_cases.move: Suggest the whole team agree on one quiet hour, since one person alone looks unresponsive.

use_cases.situation: Your kids fight over screens at dinner.
use_cases.move: Set one household rule that applies to the adults too.

pocket_idea: One family saying no leaves its child out of the group chat; an agreement made together removes that cost.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A child without a phone is left out when everyone else has one, which is why Haidt asks whole schools to act together.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Haidt says childhood was rewired between about 2010 and 2015 from outdoor play to phones, and teen anxiety rose. A single family that says no leaves its child out, so he asks schools and communities to agree on shared rules: phone-free schools, later ages and more independent play. Some researchers dispute the cause.
